```{python}
def r_horizon(a):
    """Horizon radius for spin a_*, in units of r_S."""
    return (1.0 + np.sqrt(1.0 - np.asarray(a, float) ** 2)) / 2.0


def r_ergo(a, theta):
    """Static-surface radius for spin a_* at polar angle theta, in units of r_S."""
    a = np.asarray(a, float)
    return (1.0 + np.sqrt(1.0 - a**2 * np.cos(theta) ** 2)) / 2.0


def r_isco(a):
    """ISCO radius for signed spin a_*, in units of r_S.

    The sign factor -a/|a| picks the prograde branch for a > 0 and the
    retrograde branch for a < 0. At a = 0 it is 0/0, but Z1 = 3 there so the
    square root vanishes identically and either branch gives 3 r_S.
    """
    a = np.asarray(a, float)
    Z1 = 1.0 + np.cbrt(1.0 - a**2) * (np.cbrt(1.0 + a) + np.cbrt(1.0 - a))
    Z2 = np.sqrt(3.0 * a**2 + Z1**2)
    root = np.sqrt(np.clip((3.0 - Z1) * (3.0 + Z1 + 2.0 * Z2), 0.0, None))
    sign = -np.sign(a)
    return (3.0 + Z2 + sign * root) / 2.0
```

## The Schwarzschild radius, normalized

So recall in [the previous chapter](../scales-and-schwarzschild/index.qmd) that
we can derive the Schwarzschild radius, $r_S$ by using the Newtonian expression
for escape velocity and setting it equal to $c$. This is a bit of a lie because
the Schwarzschild radius comes from the Schwarzschild solution to Einstein's
equations, which are different from Newtonian physics. They are also a lie in
another, subtle way.

Imagine Newtonian physics with a maximum speed for anything to be $c$. Now
imagine a planet with escape speed of, say, $1.1 c$. What would happen if you
had a rocket ship that could instantaneously get to $v = c$ from the ground?
The same thing that happens when you throw a ball up in the air less than the
escape speed: it goes up a bit and then comes down. And the faster you throw
it, the farther up the ball goes. So the rocket ship could go quite a ways up.
When it is far away, the escape speed is then slower, because you have a larger
value of $r$ in:

$$
v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \left(\frac{2 G M}{r}\right)^{1/2}.
$$ {#eq-vesc}

So if you get very high up, you can then fire the rocket ship again to
accelerate (up to $c$ in our made-up rules of physics) and go further away
until the ship is at $r$ large enough that $v_{\mathrm{esc}} < c$. So you could
eventually escape as long as you could keep accelerating and had enough fuel.

This is not the case for a black hole. For a black hole, space is warped and
curved such that you cannot get out. I like to think of it in an analogy to an
intersection where all streets are one-way streets pointing toward the
intersection. It is not that there is no practical way out, the laws of nature
forbid it. The boundary where you can't get past is called the "event horizon,"
and we will come back to that in a second, but first we should normalize the
Schwarzschild radius expression into useful units.

Take

$$
r_S = \frac{2 G M}{c^2}
$$ {#eq-schwarzschild}

and write it in terms of how many kilometers of radius per solar mass
($1\ M_{\odot} = 2 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}$) of black hole:

$$
r_S = 3\ \mathrm{km}\ \left(\frac{M}{M_{\odot}}\right)
$$ {#eq-rs-km}

and then for AU ($1\ \mathrm{AU} = 1.5 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{cm}$) and
hundreds of million solar masses:

$$
r_S = 2\ \mathrm{AU}\ \left(\frac{M}{10^8\ M_{\odot}}\right).
$$ {#eq-rs-au}

The one in km is good for stellar-mass black holes and one for AU is good for
supermassive black holes.

Both of these have event horizons, which I said we would get to, but first we
need to talk about another oddball quirk of black holes.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-schwarzschild}

1.  Jupiter has a mass of $1.898 \times 10^{30}\ \mathrm{g}$. Calculate its
    Schwarzschild radius, and give the answer in centimeters, in kilometers,
    and in astronomical units.

    ::: {.callout-note .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
    **Substitute into @eq-schwarzschild, and keep the units attached.** Do not
    multiply anything yet.

    $$
    \begin{aligned}
    r_S &= \frac{2GM}{c^2} \\[0.8em]
        &= \frac{2\,\left(6.674 \times 10^{-8}\
             \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\right)
             \left(1.898 \times 10^{30}\ \mathrm{g}\right)}
             {\left(2.998 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)^{2}}
    \end{aligned}
    $$

    **Now cancel the units, still without touching the numbers.** On top,
    $\mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} \times \mathrm{g} =
    \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-2}}$. On the bottom,
    $\left(\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)^2 = \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-2}}$. So the units
    of the whole expression are

    $$
    \frac{\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-2}}}{\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-2}}} = \mathrm{cm}.
    $$

    *Do the units make sense?* Centimeters are a length, and a radius is a
    length, so yes. **This is the step that catches mistakes early.** Had you
    forgotten to square $c$, the bottom would have been
    $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$ and the answer would have come out in
    $\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}}$ — not a length, and you would know something was
    wrong before doing a single multiplication.

    **Only now, the numbers.**

    $$
    r_S = \frac{2\,(6.674 \times 10^{-8})(1.898 \times 10^{30})}
               {(2.998 \times 10^{10})^{2}}\ \mathrm{cm}
        = \frac{2.533 \times 10^{23}}{8.988 \times 10^{20}}\ \mathrm{cm}
        = 282\ \mathrm{cm}.
    $$

    **The other two units are conversions, and they get the same treatment.**
    You have $282\ \mathrm{cm}$ and you want kilometers. You know that
    $1\ \mathrm{km} = 10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}$. Write that equivalence as a
    fraction — and **choose which way up by asking which arrangement cancels
    the unit you are trying to get rid of.** Here that means centimeters go in
    the denominator:

    $$
    r_S = 282\ \mathrm{cm} \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{km}}{10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}}.
    $$

    Cancel: $\mathrm{cm} \times \mathrm{km}/\mathrm{cm} = \mathrm{km}$. *Do the
    units make sense?* Kilometers are a length, so yes. **Now** multiply:

    $$
    r_S = \frac{282}{10^{5}}\ \mathrm{km} = 2.8 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{km}.
    $$

    **This is why the fraction is worth writing out rather than just dividing.**
    Had you put it the other way up, as
    $10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm} / 1\ \mathrm{km}$, nothing would have canceled and you
    would have been left with $\mathrm{cm^2\,km^{-1}}$ — not a length. The setup
    tells you whether to multiply or divide, so you never have to guess.

    Astronomical units work the same way, with
    $1\ \mathrm{AU} = 1.5 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{cm}$:

    $$
    r_S = 282\ \mathrm{cm} \times
          \frac{1\ \mathrm{AU}}{1.5 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{cm}}
        = \frac{282}{1.5 \times 10^{13}}\ \mathrm{AU}
        = 1.9 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{AU}.
    $$

    **Check it against the normalized form.** Jupiter is
    $1.898\times10^{30} / 2\times10^{33} = 9.5 \times 10^{-4}\ M_{\odot}$, so
    @eq-rs-km gives $3 \times 9.5\times10^{-4} = 2.85\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{km}$
    — agreeing with the direct calculation to about 1%. That last 1% is the
    rounding in @eq-rs-km itself, not a mistake in either route.

    Worth a moment: to make Jupiter a black hole you would have to squeeze the
    largest planet in the Solar System down to a sphere **less than three
    meters across**. You could walk past it.
    :::

2.  Calculate $r_S$ in kilometers for black holes of $5$, $15$, and
    $55\ M_{\odot}$. *(You should be able to do these in your head.)*

3.  Calculate $r_S$ in astronomical units for black holes of
    $1.0 \times 10^{6}$, $3.0 \times 10^{8}$, and
    $2 \times 10^{10}\ M_{\odot}$. *(These too.)*

:::

## The no-hair theorem

One of the fun things about studying black holes, is that the phraseology is
ridiculous and awesome. Even "black hole" is pretty cool in and of itself.
"Event horizon" is another winner. One of the fun ones is the no-hair
theorem.[Another fun one is related but pertains to neutron stars: I-Love-Q
relations.]{.aside .content-visible when-format="html"}

<!-- The no-hair attribution sentence was drafted by the assistant 2026-08-20 and
     approved by Kayhan the same day. -->
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
The phrase is John Wheeler's, from a 1971 article he wrote with Remo Ruffini
[@ruffini1971]; the theorem itself is a body of work by several people, and
Jacob Bekenstein proved some of the sharpest pieces of it [@bekenstein1972].
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
The phrase is John Wheeler's, from a 1971 article he wrote with Remo Ruffini;
the theorem itself is a body of work by several people, and Jacob Bekenstein
proved some of the sharpest pieces of it.
:::

The no-hair theorem states that once a black hole has settled after it has
formed or you add matter to it, it can be completely described by three
numbers: the mass, $M$, the spin angular momentum, $J$, and the electrical
charge, $Q$.

Astrophysically, electrical charge is not important because there are always
enough ions in space that any significant charge in a black hole would attract
opposite charges and return it to zero charge again.

We give names to different types of black holes (and the spacetimes [and the
coordinate systems of the spacetimes]) depending on whether they incorporate
$M$, $M$ & $J$, or $M$, $J$, & $Q$:

::: {.callout-note .table-view title="The four black hole spacetimes"}
| Name | Constraint | Free parameters |
|---|---|---|
| Kerr–Newman | — | $M$, $J$, $Q$ |
| Kerr | $Q = 0$ | $M$, $J$ |
| Reissner–Nordström | $J = 0$ | $M$, $Q$ |
| Schwarzschild | $Q = J = 0$ | $M$ |
:::

Note, that we usually talk about the spin of a black hole using the
dimensionless spin parameter:

$$
a_* = \frac{c J}{G M^2}.
$$ {#eq-astar}

You should check that this is dimensionless. Also note that sometimes people
use the symbol $a$ or $\chi$ or $\tilde{\chi}$ for the same thing. The reason
we do it this way is because there is a self-similarity about it. There is also
a maximum amount of angular momentum a black hole can have so that the
dimensionless spin parameter can only take on values $-1 < a_* < 1$, where the
negative sign means spinning "backward" from whatever coordinate system we
have defined.

<!-- The extremal-limit clause was drafted by the assistant 2026-08-20 and
     approved by Kayhan the same day. -->
The end points are a limit rather than a value: a black hole can be spun
arbitrarily close to $|a_*| = 1$ but never quite to it, so when we quote a
result "at $a_* = 1$" we mean the value it approaches. Such a black hole is
called *extremal*. (More later!)

Anyway, back to the hairlessness of black holes. Once the black hole has
settled down, it does not matter if you filled it with buckeyes or (poor)
wolverines as long as you filled it with the same amount of mass and angular
momentum (and charge). From the outside, they look the same. So they have no
"hair," a metaphor for anything other than those three quantities.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## The event horizon

The event horizon is a mathematical surface. It is not a physical surface just
as the equator around the Earth is not a physical line but a mathematical line
/ boundary.

The event horizon is the surface of no return. Once something goes past the
event horizon, it is impossible for it to escape. Nothing, not even light, can
escape. In fact, no *information* (in the physics sense) can get out except for
$M$, $J$, & $Q$.

::: {.callout-note title="Why is it called an event horizon?"}
As we shall see when we get more into relativity, an event is a point in
spacetime. It has spatial location and a moment in time. A horizon is something
you can't see past. If you look out at the ocean (or Lake Michigan?) you can't
see any ships beyond the horizon. In this case it is caused by the curvature of
the Earth. In the case of a black hole, you have no access to the spacetime on
the other side of the horizon because no information comes out.
:::

Okay, where is this surface? For a Schwarzschild black hole, that surface is a
sphere with radius $r_S$. See? There was a reason we spent so much time
calculating it. So that's how close you can get to a non-spinning black hole
without saying goodbye to the rest of the Universe. For a spinning black hole,
you can get closer! Let's talk about spinning black holes specifically now.

## Spinning black holes

For me, spinning black holes really showed that general relativity is very
different from Newtonian gravity plus special relativity. Of course there are
no horizons in Newtonian gravity. So we have already learned about something
inexplicable without GR. But when a black hole has significant spin angular
momentum, its spin *drags* spacetime around it. You can think of a
Schwarzschild black hole as *pulling* spacetime into it. Once you are inside
the horizon, you *have* to go toward the center of the black hole (where there
is a singularity). For spinning black holes there is another region called:

### The ergosphere

The ergosphere is not a sphere. It is a oblate spheroidal region. The degree of
oblateness depends on the magnitude of $a_*$. Just as inside the Schwarzschild
radius of a non-rotating black hole, you have to go toward the center of the
black hole, inside the ergosphere you have to orbit in the same direction as
the black hole's spin. Even if you pointed a laser pointer in the opposite
direction, the light would move in the same direction as the spin.

This effect is called *frame dragging*. The effect of gravity is such that a
massive spinning object twists spacetime in the same direction. It is
theoretically possible to extract energy from this region. This is why it is
called "ergo" (from the Greek word $\epsilon\rho\gamma\omicron$, I think,
meaning work). We will come back to this.

Also worth noting is that the outer surface of the ergosphere is sometimes
called the static surface (or static limit).

The horizon radius for arbitrary spin is

$$
r_H = \frac{r_S + r_S\sqrt{1 - a_*^2}}{2}.
$$ {#eq-rh}

What's that? You want to know what the static surface equation is? Sure!

$$
r_E = \frac{r_S + r_S\sqrt{1 - a_*^2 \cos^2\theta}}{2}.
$$ {#eq-re}

It touches the horizon at $\theta = 0, \pi$ (at the poles).

```{python}
#| label: fig-ergosphere
#| fig-cap: "The ergosphere is not a sphere. At three spins, the static surface (@eq-re, solid) drawn against the horizon (@eq-rh, dashed) in the same color. Both are in units of $r_S$, and the picture is a slice through the spin axis, which runs vertically. The static surface always reaches $r_S$ at the equator no matter the spin; the horizon shrinks as the spin rises, so the gap between them opens up. The two meet only at the poles."
#| fig-alt: "A polar cross-section through a spinning black hole, with the spin axis vertical. Three pairs of nested closed curves are drawn in different colors, one pair for each spin value 0.3, 0.6 and 0.95. In each pair a solid curve marks the static surface and a dashed curve of the same color marks the horizon. Every solid curve passes through the same point on the horizontal equator at one Schwarzschild radius, while the dashed horizon circles get smaller as spin increases, from nearly touching at spin 0.3 to a much smaller circle at spin 0.95. Each solid curve is pinched inward at the top and bottom so that it meets its own dashed circle exactly on the vertical axis at the poles."

# figsize is NOT portable between documents: bbox_inches='tight' crops by an
# amount that depends on this figure's own labels, so the invariant to match
# is PAINTED width, not figsize. Swept and measured: 5.2in paints 558 css px,
# beside lecture 3's square fig-spacetime at 551. Column is 699px here (663

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 5.2))

theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 721)
spins = [(0.30, BLUE, "-"), (0.60, ORANGE, "-"), (0.95, AQUA, "-")]

for a, color, style in spins:
    rE = r_ergo(a, theta)
    ax.plot(rE * np.sin(theta), rE * np.cos(theta),
            color=color, linestyle=style, label=rf"$a_* = {a:g}$", zorder=3)
    rH = r_horizon(a)
    ax.plot(rH * np.sin(theta), rH * np.cos(theta),

ax.axvline(0.0, color=AXIS, linewidth=0.8, zorder=1)

ax.set_ylabel(r"$r/r_S$, along the spin axis")
ax.set_xlim(-1.35, 1.35)
ax.set_ylim(-1.35, 1.35)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.grid(False)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=10)
plt.show()
```

### The ISCO

::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

#### Physical intuition

There is another interesting concept with black holes, called the Innermost
Stable Circular Orbit (ISCO). In Newtonian gravity, no matter where you put an
orbiting particle around a massive object, it can have a circular orbit. What's
more, it is stable. If you poke the orbit, it will become an eccentric orbit,
moving slightly closer and slightly further away, but it will continue to
orbit.

General relativity becomes Newtonian gravity in the limit of weak gravity (far
away, low-mass, slow-moving). So it still predicts Earth's orbit around the
Sun. But there are places where GR predicts things that Newtonian gravity
doesn't. Close to a black hole, gravity — in a sense — is stronger according to
Einstein than according to Newton.[It should be noted that this is a very
Newtonian way of thinking about it, but that's okay. We are building up
intuition here.]{.aside .content-visible when-format="html"} So if you poke a
circular orbit around a black hole, it would go further and closer, but when it
got closer, it wouldn't be able to get further out again. It would go in, and
in, and in, and in. So if a butterfly sneezes, the orbiting body would spiral
in toward the black hole.

#### Mathematical explanation

This effect takes place inside a specific radius that is called the radius of
the innermost stable circular orbit $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}}$. What is the value of
$r_{\mathrm{ISCO}}$? It depends on the spin of the black hole. For $a_* = 0$,
$r_{\mathrm{ISCO}} = 3 r_S$. For $a_* = 1$, $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}} = 0.5 r_S$. And
for $a_* = -1$, $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}} = 4.5 r_S$. This means that the faster a
black hole is spinning the "easier" it is to continue orbiting in a circular
orbit in the same direction. But the harder it is to orbit in the opposite
direction. The exact functional form is a little complicated, but it is:

$$
r_{\mathrm{ISCO}} = \frac{GM}{c^2}\left(3 + Z_2
  - \frac{a_*}{|a_*|}\sqrt{(3 - Z_1)(3 + Z_1 + 2 Z_2)}\right),
$$ {#eq-isco}

<!-- The sign-factor paragraph was drafted by the assistant 2026-08-20 and
     approved by Kayhan the same day. -->
where the factor $-a_*/|a_*|$ does nothing but set the sign: it is $-1$ for a
prograde orbit ($a_* > 0$) and $+1$ for a retrograde one ($a_* < 0$), so the
sign of the spin parameter now carries the direction of the orbit all by
itself. Everything else in the formula depends only on $a_*^2$ and on
$(1 \pm a_*)^{1/3}$ in a combination that is unchanged when $a_*$ flips sign,
which is why the sign factor has to be put in by hand. At $a_* = 0$ the factor
is undefined, but it does not matter: $Z_1 = 3$ there, the square root is
exactly zero, and both choices give the same $3 r_S$. The other two quantities
are

$$
Z_1 = 1 + (1 - a_*^2)^{1/3}\left( (1 + a_*)^{1/3} + (1 - a_*)^{1/3}\right),
$$ {#eq-z1}

and

$$
Z_2 = (3 a_*^2 + Z_1^2)^{1/2}.
$$ {#eq-z2}

#### Numerical exploration

The formula in @eq-isco is much easier to trust once you have watched it
produce the three numbers quoted above. Here it is, evaluated across
the whole range of spins.

```{python}
#| label: isco-ladder

import numpy as np


def r_isco_over_rs(a):
    """ISCO radius for signed spin a_*, in units of r_S."""
    Z1 = 1.0 + np.cbrt(1.0 - a**2) * (np.cbrt(1.0 + a) + np.cbrt(1.0 - a))
    Z2 = np.sqrt(3.0 * a**2 + Z1**2)
    root = np.sqrt(max((3.0 - Z1) * (3.0 + Z1 + 2.0 * Z2), 0.0))
    sign = -np.sign(a)
    return (3.0 + Z2 + sign * root) / 2.0


spins = [-1.0, -0.9, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.998, 1.0]

for a in spins:
    direction = "retrograde" if a < 0 else ("prograde" if a > 0 else "either")
    print(f"a* = {a:+6.3f}   r_ISCO = {r_isco_over_rs(a):6.3f} r_S   {direction}")
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: isco-ladder-live

import numpy as np


def r_isco_over_rs(a):
    """ISCO radius for signed spin a_*, in units of r_S."""
    Z1 = 1.0 + np.cbrt(1.0 - a**2) * (np.cbrt(1.0 + a) + np.cbrt(1.0 - a))
    Z2 = np.sqrt(3.0 * a**2 + Z1**2)
    root = np.sqrt(max((3.0 - Z1) * (3.0 + Z1 + 2.0 * Z2), 0.0))
    sign = -np.sign(a)
    return (3.0 + Z2 + sign * root) / 2.0


spins = [-1.0, -0.9, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.998, 1.0]  # <- edit this list

for a in spins:
    direction = "retrograde" if a < 0 else ("prograde" if a > 0 else "either")
    print(f"a* = {a:+6.3f}   r_ISCO = {r_isco_over_rs(a):6.3f} r_S   {direction}")
```

:::

Prograde orbits are to the right of center and retrograde to the left, and the curve is markedly steeper on the prograde side: almost all of the drop from $3\\,r_S$ to $0.5\\,r_S$ happens above $a_* = 0.9$. The three values quoted in the text are marked."

It is gently sloped on the left, retrograde, half and becomes very steep near the right end, so most of the descent from 3 to 0.5 is concentrated in the last tenth of the spin range. Three points are marked with dots and labels at spin minus one, zero, and plus one."

```{python}
            markeredgewidth=1.2, linestyle="none", zorder=4)
    ax.annotate(label, xy=(a0, y0), xytext=(0, 10), textcoords="offset points",

ax.axvline(0.0, color=AXIS, linewidth=0.8, zorder=1)

ax.annotate("prograde", xy=(0.5, 0.25), color=MUTED, fontsize=10, ha="center")

ax.set_xlabel(r"$a_* = cJ/GM^2$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$r_{\mathrm{ISCO}}\,/\,r_S$")
ax.set_xlim(-1.05, 1.05)
ax.set_ylim(0.0, 5.0)
plt.show()
```

Because you can get closer to a spinning black hole, you can get more energy out
of the black hole. This is important for understanding the black holes that we
can see because of how much matter they are pulling into them.

    $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}} = 3\,r_S$ for a non-spinning black hole.

2.  Now show that $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}} = 0.5\,r_S$ for a maximally spinning black
    hole with the orbit going the same way as the spin.

3.  What spin gives a black hole an innermost stable circular orbit at exactly
    twice its Schwarzschild radius, $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}} = 2\,r_S$? There is no
    tidy way to invert @eq-isco by hand, so this one is a computation rather
    than an algebra problem.

    ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
    Three routes, and any of them is a real answer:

    * **Read it off @fig-isco.** Find $2\,r_S$ on the vertical axis, follow
      across to the curve, and drop down to the spin axis. That gets you the
      first digit and tells you roughly where to look.
    * **Use the Turn the knobs cell above**, iteratively. Put a spin in the
      list, look at whether $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}}$ came out above or below
      $2\,r_S$, and use that to choose the next one. Each round should let you
      pin down one more digit — this is a perfectly respectable way to solve an
      equation you cannot rearrange, and it is what the cell is there for.
    * **Write your own program.** Whatever language you like: evaluate

Wow, we are learning a lot about black holes! I hope I get through this in one
lecture! What happens if we get close to a black hole? Will we get shredded to
pieces? Let's find out.

## Tidal forces

::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

### Physical intuition

What is tidal force? It is a force that is different from one side of a body
compared to the other. If I pull on both your head and feet equally, you just
move. If I pull very hard on your feet and only a little bit on your head, then
you will move but also get stretched. If I pull harder than your body can hold
itself together (tensile strength), then you become *disrupted*.

### Mathematical explanation

Let's find the tidal force of gravity by a large mass $M$ acting on a smaller
mass $m$. The distance from the center of mass $M$ to the center of mass $m$ is
$d$ and the size of the small mass is $s = 2\Delta r$. What is the difference in
forces between the gravitational pull on one side versus the other side of $m$?
It's:

$$
F_t = - \frac{G M m}{(d - \Delta r)^2} + \frac{G M m}{(d + \Delta r)^2}.
$$ {#eq-tidal-raw}

We are going to make things easy for ourselves and assume that
$\Delta r \ll d$ as well as only consider tidal forces in the radial direction.
That is, we aren't considering tidal forces on a flying saucer landing on
Earth. We are only considering tidal forces on a tall tree on Earth.

We do a little rearranging and find that

$$
F_t = -\frac{G M m}{d^2} \left[ \frac{1}{(1 - \Delta r / d)^2}
  - \frac{1}{(1 + \Delta r / d)^2} \right].
$$ {#eq-tidal-rearranged}

Next, we use the fact that $(1 + x)^y \approx 1 + y x$ for $x \ll 1$ to write

$$
F_t = -\frac{G M m}{d^2} \left[ (1 + 2 \Delta r / d)
  - (1 - 2 \Delta r / d) \right].
$$ {#eq-tidal-binomial}

Collect things and ignore the sign at the front because we are only interested
in the magnitude of the difference:

$$
F_t = \frac{2 G M m}{d^3} s.
$$ {#eq-tidal}

### Numerical exploration

@eq-tidal has an $m$ in it, which is awkward for comparing one victim to
another. Divide it out and what is left is a tidal *acceleration*,
$a_t = 2GMs/d^3$, which depends only on the black hole and on how long you are.
Here it is at the horizon, where $d = r_S$, for a person-sized body.

```{python}
#| label: tidal-ladder

from astropy import constants as const
from astropy import units as u


def a_tidal(M, d, s):
    """Tidal acceleration across a body of length s at distance d from mass M."""
    return (2 * const.G * M * s / d**3).to(u.m / u.s**2)


def r_S(M):
    """Schwarzschild radius for a mass M."""
    return (2 * const.G * M / const.c**2).to(u.km)


person = 1.8 * u.m

for M in [10, 100, 1e4, 1e6, 4.3e6, 1e9] * const.M_sun:
    at = a_tidal(M, r_S(M), person)
    print(f"M = {M.to(u.M_sun).value:9.1e} Msun   "
          f"r_S = {r_S(M):>11.4g}   "
          f"a_t = {(at / const.g0).decompose().value:9.2e} g")
```

:::

<!-- This Resolution callout, and its title was drafted by the assistant 2026-08-20 and
     approved by Kayhan the same day. -->
::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about what the strongest tidal force possible is for fixed $m$ and $s$."}
We want the biggest value of $M / d^3$. Well the closest you can get to an
object is its radius. So you want the object to be compact to have a big tidal
force. What's a compact, massive object? A black hole! So the maximum tidal
force possible is the tidal force at the horizon of a black hole.
:::

Now let's consider how this tidal force scales with mass when at the horizon:

$$
F_t \propto \frac{M}{r_S^3}.
$$ {#eq-tidal-horizon}

And using the fact that $r_S \propto M$, we get:

$$
F_t \propto \frac{M}{M^3} = \frac{1}{M^2}.
$$ {#eq-tidal-scaling}

The tidal force is *smaller* when the black hole is *bigger*! This will come
into play when we discuss tidal disruption events (TDEs). If you *have* to go
into a black hole and have your choice of which one, choose the biggest one you
can find. At least you'll survive going through the horizon. Then you'll get
spaghettified inside on your way to the singularity.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Try it yourself {#sec-interactive-tidal}

<!-- This lead-in and the How to use it callout was drafted by the assistant 2026-08-20 and
     approved by Kayhan the same day. -->

The figure below is live. There are only two things to change — how far out the
body is, and how heavy the black hole is — and the whole of this section is in
what happens when you change one and not the other.

Drag the body inward and the tidal acceleration climbs as $d^{-3}$; that much
you would expect. Now park it on the horizon and drag the *mass* instead. The
picture does not move at all — the horizon is drawn at $d/r_S = 1$ whatever the
black hole weighs — and yet the acceleration falls by twelve orders of
magnitude. That is @eq-tidal-scaling, and it is much stranger to watch than it
is to read.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How to use it"}
* **Drag** the orange body to move it. It settles onto the horizon when you
  bring it close, so you can park there without a steady hand.
* **The mass slider** runs from $1$ to $10^{9}\ M_{\odot}$, with a tick at every
  decade. Watch the scale bar under the diagram as you drag it: the picture
  stays put while the physical size of that same circle runs from a few
  kilometers to a few billion.
* **Keyboard:** Tab to the body, then use the arrow keys to move it in and out.
  Hold <kbd>Shift</kbd> for larger steps, or use <kbd>Home</kbd> and
  <kbd>End</kbd> for the two extremes. The arrow keys stop at the horizon and
  will not take you through it.
* **Fall in** pushes the body through the horizon — as does simply dragging it
  well inside. It falls to the center and stays there, the readouts stop
  meaning anything, and **Reset** is the only way to get it back. That is the
  one thing about an event horizon worth feeling rather than being told.
* Switch the falling body to **a Sun-like star** and the question changes from
  what the tide *feels* like to whether the star survives it at all. Find the
  mass where the verdict changes.

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-tidal}

Throughout, take a person to be $s = 1.8\ \mathrm{m}$ tall, take Earth's
gravitational acceleration to be $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, and use
$r_S = 3\ \mathrm{km}\,(M/M_{\odot})$ from @eq-rs-km. Answers are quoted to two
significant figures, which is enough that the rounding in $r_S$ does not
matter. The interactive figure above is a good way to check yourself.

1.  Sagittarius A\*, the black hole at the center of our own Galaxy, has
    $M = 4.3 \times 10^{6}\ M_{\odot}$. Calculate the tidal acceleration across
    a person at its event horizon, and express it in units of $g$.

    ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
    @eq-tidal gives a *force*. To turn it into the acceleration you want, use
    $F_t = m\,a_t$ and set that equal to @eq-tidal — the $m$ cancels, leaving
    $a_t = 2GMs/d^3$, which depends on the black hole and on how long you are
    but not on your mass at all. Evaluate it at the horizon, $d = r_S$, then
    divide by $g$ to express the result in Earth gravities.
    :::

    ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
    $a_t \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\ g$. You would cross the horizon of our
    Galaxy's black hole without feeling a thing.
    :::

2.  The tidal acceleration across a person at the horizon of a
    $10\ M_{\odot}$ black hole is $1.9 \times 10^{7}\ g$. Chani wants the
    value for a $10^{6}\ M_{\odot}$ black hole and starts substituting into
    @eq-tidal all over again. Paul says she does not need to. Get the answer
    Paul's way, in one line.

    ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
    At the horizon, and only at the horizon, @eq-tidal-scaling applies: $a_t$
    depends on nothing but $M^{-2}$. So the ratio of the two accelerations is
    fixed by the ratio of the two masses alone, and you never need $G$, $c$ or
    $s$ at all.
    :::

    ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
    $a_t \approx 1.9 \times 10^{-3}\ g$ — a factor of $10^{10}$ smaller, because
    the mass went up by $10^{5}$ and $a_t \propto 1/M^{2}$.
    :::

3.  What is the smallest black hole whose event horizon a person could cross
    intact? Take $10\ g$ as the most a body could withstand for more than a
    moment.

    ::: {.callout-note .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
    Start from @eq-tidal as an acceleration, $a_t = 2GMs/d^3$, and evaluate it
    at the horizon, $d = r_S = 2GM/c^2$:

    $$
    a_t = \frac{2GMs}{\left(2GM/c^2\right)^3}
        = \frac{2GMs\,c^6}{8G^3M^3}
        = \frac{s\,c^6}{4G^2M^2},
    $$

    which is @eq-tidal-scaling with the constants kept. Setting $a_t = 10g$ and
    solving for $M$,

    $$
    M = \sqrt{\frac{s\,c^6}{4G^2\,(10g)}}.
    $$

    **Check the units before substituting anything.** Inside the root,

    $$
    \frac{\mathrm{cm}\;\left(\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)^{6}}
         {\left(\mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\right)^{2}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-2}}}
    = \frac{\mathrm{cm^{7}\,s^{-6}}}
           {\mathrm{cm^{7}\,g^{-2}\,s^{-6}}}
    = \mathrm{g^{2}},
    $$

    and the square root of that is $\mathrm{g}$. *Do the units make sense?* A
    mass in grams is what we solved for, so yes. **Now** put the numbers in,
    converting the height the same way, with
    $1\ \mathrm{m} = 100\ \mathrm{cm}$:

    $$
    s = 1.8\ \mathrm{m} \times \frac{100\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{m}}
      = 180\ \mathrm{cm},
    $$

    which gives $M \approx 2.7 \times 10^{37}\ \mathrm{g}$. Grams are awkward
    for a black hole, so convert once more, with
    $1\ M_{\odot} = 2 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}$:

    $$
    M = 2.7 \times 10^{37}\ \mathrm{g} \times
        \frac{1\ M_{\odot}}{2 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}
      \approx 1.4 \times 10^{4}\ M_{\odot}.
    $$

    **The number itself is not the lesson.** Because $M \propto a_t^{-1/2}$,
    the answer barely moves when you change your mind about what a body can
    take: $1\,g$ gives $4.3\times10^{4}\ M_{\odot}$ and $1000\,g$ gives
    $1.4\times10^{3}\ M_{\odot}$. Every reasonable threshold lands in the same
    place — the **intermediate-mass** range, thousands to tens of thousands of
    solar masses. Surviving a horizon crossing is not a matter of being careful;
    it requires a whole class of black hole.
    :::

4.  A star is torn apart when the tide across it beats the gravity holding it
    together. That happens inside the star's **tidal radius**,

    $$
    R_T = R_*\left(\frac{2M}{M_*}\right)^{1/3},
    $$ {#eq-tidal-radius}

    where $M_*$ and $R_*$ are the star's mass and radius and $M$ is the black
    hole's mass.

    ::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="How to derive the tidal radius expression"}
    Divide @eq-tidal by $m$ to get an acceleration, and put $s = R_*$: that is
    the tide between the star's center and its surface, which is the half of
    the star its own gravity has to hold on to.

    $$
    a_{\mathrm{tide}} = \frac{2GMR_*}{r^3}
    \qquad\text{against}\qquad
    g_* = \frac{GM_*}{R_*^2},
    $$

    the star's own gravitational acceleration at its surface. The star comes
    apart where the tide wins, so set them equal:

    $$
    \frac{2GMR_*}{r^3} = \frac{GM_*}{R_*^2}
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    r^3 = \frac{2MR_*^3}{M_*}
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    r = R_*\left(\frac{2M}{M_*}\right)^{1/3}.
    $$

    *Do the units make sense?* The ratio $M/M_*$ is a mass over a mass, so it
    is a pure number, and a pure number raised to any power is still a pure
    number. That leaves $R_T$ with the units of $R_*$ — a length, which is what
    a radius must be. The check is quick here because the algebra was done in
    symbols, but it is the same habit: **satisfy yourself about the units
    before you put any numbers in.**

    Using the star's full diameter instead of its radius would compare the two
    *ends* of the star to each other rather than the surface to the center, and
    would put a $4$ where the $2$ is.
    :::

    A star is only disrupted if $R_T$ lies *outside* the horizon — otherwise it
    crosses intact and no one ever sees it come apart. Using a Sun-like star
    ($R_* = R_{\odot} = 7.0 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{km}$, $M_* = M_{\odot}$),
    find the smallest black hole mass for which a star can cross the event
    horizon without being disrupted.

    ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
    You want the mass at which $R_T = r_S$. Write both in terms of $M$ — one
    from @eq-tidal-radius, one from @eq-rs-km — and solve. Note
    $R_T \propto M^{1/3}$ while $r_S \propto M$, so the ratio $R_T/r_S$ *falls*
    as the black hole gets bigger, which is why there is a largest hole that
    can still shred a star rather than a smallest one.
    :::

    ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
    $M \approx 1.6 \times 10^{8}\ M_{\odot}$. Above this mass a Sun-like star
    goes through the horizon whole — the same story as exercise 3, one rung up
    the ladder of victims.
    :::

5.  Repeat exercise 4 for a **white dwarf**, with $R = 0.013\,R_{\odot}$ and
    $M = 0.6\,M_{\odot}$. Which black holes can tear one apart, and which
    swallow it whole? Astronomers care about the answer: it is why a disrupted
    white dwarf is evidence for a black hole of a particular size.

:::

## Capstone {#sec-capstone}

<!-- The lead-in below is the assistant's wording; the three problems are
     Kayhan's spec. -->

These three pull the whole lecture together: the ISCO, the tidal radius, and
the Schwarzschild radius all in one place. Take them slowly, and keep the units
attached the whole way through.

Write the ISCO radius of @eq-isco as

$$
r_{\mathrm{ISCO}} = \frac{GM}{c^2}\,f(a_*),
$$ {#eq-isco-f}

where $f(a_*)$ is the whole complicated bracket — everything in @eq-isco except
the leading $GM/c^2$. It is a pure number that depends only on the spin.

1.  A star that wanders too close to a black hole is torn apart at its tidal
    radius, @eq-tidal-radius, and swallowed once it is inside the innermost
    stable circular orbit. For a given star and a given spin there is one black
    hole mass at which those two radii coincide. Find an expression for it.

    ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
    Set @eq-isco-f equal to @eq-tidal-radius:

    $$
    \frac{GM}{c^2}f(a_*) = R_*\left(\frac{2M}{M_*}\right)^{1/3}.
    $$

    Both sides carry $M$, so collect them. Dividing by $M^{1/3}$ leaves
    $M^{2/3}$ on the left, and raising both sides to the power $3/2$ gives

    $$
    M = \left(\frac{2}{M_*}\right)^{1/2}
        \left(\frac{R_*\,c^2}{G\,f(a_*)}\right)^{3/2}.
    $$

    *Do the units make sense?* Inside the second bracket,
    $\mathrm{cm}\,(\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-2}}) / (\mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}})
    = \mathrm{g}$, so that bracket is $\mathrm{g^{3/2}}$. The first bracket is
    $\mathrm{g^{-1/2}}$. Their product is $\mathrm{g}$ — a mass, which is what
    was asked for.
    :::

2.  Evaluate that expression for an ordinary star of one solar mass
    ($M_* = 2 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}$,
    $R_* = 7.0 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm}$) orbiting a black hole with
    $a_* = 0.5$. You will need $f(0.5)$, which you can get from @eq-isco.

3.  Now the other end of the story. A black hole can only be *seen* to disrupt a
    star if the disruption happens outside the horizon — otherwise the star goes
    in whole and nobody watches it come apart. Find the largest **non-spinning**
    black hole that can tidally disrupt a star of two solar masses, taking its
    radius to be $2\,R_{\odot} = 1.4 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{cm}$.

    ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
    The disruption is just visible when the tidal radius sits exactly at the
    horizon, so set @eq-tidal-radius equal to $r_S$. You do not need a new
    calculation: $r_S = 2GM/c^2$, so **the horizon is @eq-isco-f with
    $f = 2$** — put $f(a_*) = 2$ into your answer to the first question.
    :::

    ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
    $M \approx 3.2 \times 10^{8}\ M_{\odot}$.

    Compare it with the $1.6 \times 10^{8}\ M_{\odot}$ you found in
    @sec-exercises-tidal for a Sun-like star. The same criterion, one star twice
    as massive and twice as wide, and the answer doubles. Every black hole
    heavier than this swallows such a star whole.
    :::

:::

## Summary

| Quantity | Expression | What to remember |
|---|---|---|
| Schwarzschild radius | $r_S = \dfrac{2GM}{c^2}$ | $3\ \mathrm{km}$ per $M_{\odot}$; $2\ \mathrm{AU}$ per $10^8 M_{\odot}$ |
| No-hair theorem | $M$, $J$, $Q$ | Three numbers describe a settled black hole completely. $Q \approx 0$ astrophysically |
| Spin parameter | $a_* = \dfrac{cJ}{GM^2}$ | Dimensionless, $-1 < a_* < 1$; negative means retrograde |
| Horizon | $r_H = \dfrac{r_S}{2}\left(1 + \sqrt{1 - a_*^2}\right)$ | Shrinks as spin rises: $r_S$ at $a_* = 0$, half that at $|a_*| = 1$ |
| Static surface | $r_E = \dfrac{r_S}{2}\left(1 + \sqrt{1 - a_*^2\cos^2\theta}\right)$ | Always $r_S$ at the equator whatever the spin; meets the horizon only at the poles |
| Ergosphere | between $r_H$ and $r_E$ | Frame dragging: inside it you *must* orbit with the spin |
| ISCO | @eq-isco | $3r_S$ at $a_* = 0$, $0.5r_S$ prograde extremal, $4.5r_S$ retrograde extremal |
| Tidal force | $F_t = \dfrac{2GMms}{d^3}$ | Falls as $d^{-3}$; proportional to how long you are |
| Tidal force at a horizon | $F_t \propto \dfrac{1}{M^2}$ | **Bigger black hole, gentler crossing.** The counterintuitive one |
